tldr: This research enables humanoids to traverse stairs and obstacles without retraining or modifying a pre-trained whole-body motion tracker at all, simply by adding geometry-conditioned residual corrections to the lower-body joints. Real-world rough terrain traversal using onboard depth and unmodified reference motions was demonstrated on a Unitree G1.
hero_caption: The overall GRAFT framework. Top: A frozen behavior foundation model (BFM) outputs whole-body target joint positions from nominal motion commands, while a lightweight adapter outputs corrections for the lower body only using onboard depth cameras and adds them together. Bottom: The training flow, where a teacher model is trained with reinforcement learning using privileged elevation maps and then distilled into a student model that takes onboard depth as input.
overview:
In recent years, humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) trained on diverse human motion datasets have gained significant attention. A BFM serves as a whole-body tracking policy; simply providing kinematic reference motions allows it to generate coordinated joint commands driven by teleoperation or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing BFMs are trained almost exclusively on flat ground. As a result, when faced with uneven terrain like stairs, they fail to adjust foot swing clearance or contact timing, causing them to trip and fall.

Conventional approaches to address this issue either retrain the entire model using paired terrain-motion datasets or fine-tune it alongside a perception encoder. However, this incurs substantial computational costs, risks degrading general whole-body motion capabilities, and couples ordinary flat-ground tracking directly to the perception pipeline.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation method that keeps the original BFM completely frozen and adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to the lower-body target joint angles. Whole-body coordination and nominal locomotion generation are left to the competent BFM, allowing the adapter to focus solely on fine-tuning foot placement to clear obstacles. Furthermore, they introduce regularization to suppress corrections on flat ground and a gating mechanism to instantly switch residual intervention on or off.

In simulation, the method successfully traversed stairs and platforms across four different BFMs. Additionally, physical deployment on a compact Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrated that it could traverse stairs and platforms using onboard depth cameras while taking unmodified walking reference motions as input.
contributions: Proposed GRAFT, a lightweight adaptation framework that adds geometry-conditioned residual corrections to lower-body joint commands while keeping the pre-trained motion tracker frozen.
Introduced a regularization reward to suppress unnecessary intervention on flat ground and a gating mechanism to instantly enable or disable the residual at runtime.
Demonstrated the generality of the framework by training adapters across four distinct BFMs (SONIC, Humanoid-GPT, HoloMotion, and ScaleBFM) under a unified setup.
Distilled a teacher trained on privileged elevation maps into a student using onboard depth, validating rough terrain traversal with unmodified reference motions on a physical humanoid (Unitree G1).

sections.heading: Why do capable humanoid foundation models trip on stairs?
sections.summary: Humanoid foundation trackers trained on large-scale motion data cannot adapt to terrain because they only know flat-ground motion. This section explains the motivation and core philosophy of GRAFT, which freezes the original model and adds terrain corrections exclusively to the lower body.
sections.details:
Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) learn whole-body tracking policies from large-scale human motion datasets. They share a common interface that accepts kinematic references (target joint and body motions) from upstream sources, meaning recorded motion clips, teleoperation, or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can all drive the same BFM.

However, these motion datasets are recorded almost entirely on flat, obstacle-free ground. Consequently, while BFMs can geometrically imitate reference motions, they lack explicit mechanisms to raise foot height or adjust contact timing according to the local ground. Even when given a stair-climbing motion reference, they simply execute the movement in mid-air and fail to climb real steps, inevitably tripping.

Existing solutions either retrain the model from scratch using paired terrain and motion datasets, or fine-tune the entire model together with a terrain encoder. This demands vast data processing and compute, and risks corrupting the versatile whole-body motion priors already acquired.

To solve this, the authors propose GRAFT (Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers). The key insight is to keep the original BFM completely frozen while adding terrain-conditioned corrections (residuals) only to the lower-body execution targets. Upstream commands for the upper body remain exactly as intended by teleoperation or VLA planners, while only foot placement is adjusted by the adapter. Furthermore, a gating mechanism can completely disconnect the residual at runtime, cleanly separating stable flat-ground tracking from terrain adaptation.

sections.heading: Prior work: Balancing whole-body control and terrain adaptation
sections.summary: This section reviews three lines of prior work: whole-body motion tracking, terrain-aware locomotion, and residual learning. GRAFT stands out by preserving the reference motion interface of a frozen foundation model while achieving terrain adaptation as an additive residual on the lower body.
sections.details:
### Whole-Body Motion Tracking and Behavior Foundation Models
Whole-body motion learning has evolved from single-clip imitation into large models trained on diverse motion datasets. Notable examples include SONIC, which operates on latent commands, and Humanoid-GPT and HoloMotion, which target zero-shot tracking of unseen motions. While these serve as general-purpose interfaces separating upstream planning from low-level control, their training on flat ground prevents them from acquiring terrain-aware foot placement.

### Terrain-Aware Whole-Body Control
Locomotion using depth or elevation maps has long been studied in quadrupeds and humanoid parkour. However, these systems typically accept base velocity or navigation goals, lacking an interface to reproduce specific whole-body motions. While some efforts integrate terrain into BFMs (such as GigaBrain-WBC, GRAIL, and Perceptive BFM), they either lack external perception or fine-tune perception together with tracker weights. This creates a risk where noisy perception can compromise nominal tracking.

### Residual Adaptation of Frozen Policies
Training a residual policy on top of a fixed controller (such as ResMimic or MOSAIC) is known to prevent catastrophic forgetting. However, conventional methods primarily target object manipulation states or system failures. GRAFT introduces a distinct formulation by taking local terrain geometry as input, targeting only lower-body joint angles as output, and operating as a plug-and-play component that can be switched on or off at runtime.

sections.heading: A two-tier mechanism: Preserving whole-body tracking while fixing foot placement
sections.summary: This section covers GRAFT's architecture and training methodology. It adds lower-body-only corrections to the frozen BFM's outputs, trains them with swing clearance, edge contact, and flat-ground suppression rewards, and distills privileged elevation features into onboard depth.
sections.details:
The core philosophy of GRAFT is dividing responsibilities between whole-body motion generation and terrain execution adaptation. The overall system architecture is shown in Figure F2.

### Control and Interface Design
At each control step, the frozen BFM $\pi$ outputs whole-body target joint positions $a^0_t$ based on kinematic references and proprioception. The residual policy $f_\phi$ runs at the same control frequency (50 Hz) and outputs corrections. The final execution command is formed as:
$$a^{\mathrm{exec}}_t = a^0_t + m \odot \Delta a_t$$
where $m$ is a binary mask set to 1 for lower-body joints and 0 for upper-body joints. As a result, the BFM's upper-body commands pass through unchanged, directly executing the intent of the teleoperator or high-level planner. The adapter does not look directly at upstream references; it observes the nominal action $a^0_t$ output by the BFM, proprioception, past correction history, and local terrain geometry. During deployment, a gating switch can completely cut off the residual to revert instantly to the BFM's standalone behavior.

### Reward Design for Terrain Adaptation
The adapter is trained with base task progress and regularization rewards, alongside three specialized foot penalties:
- **Swing Clearance**: Accumulates penalties whenever foot height falls below the terrain surface plus a margin $\delta$ across all steps from lift-off to touchdown. Evaluating the entire swing phase rather than just touchdown encourages the robot to pull its feet high before stepping onto obstacles.
- **Edges and Overhangs**: Evaluates sample points $\mathcal{P}_i$ across the foot sole and penalizes the robot when a loaded foot lands on an edge or overhangs a step, guiding it toward secure footing.
- **Flat-Ground Suppression**: Computes ground flatness from the elevation variance and mean elevation differences under and ahead of the robot, penalizing correction magnitude $\rho_t$ more heavily on flat terrain. This keeps corrections near zero on flat surfaces, preserving the BFM's original gait quality.

### Teacher–Student Distillation
Training is conducted in two stages. In the first stage (privileged teacher), the adapter is trained using PPO with accurate local elevation maps from simulation. In the second stage (onboard depth student), the trained teacher is frozen, and a student network is distilled using mean squared error loss to predict teacher actions from onboard depth images rendered from the robot's perspective. This enables direct deployment using the physical robot's onboard depth camera.

sections.heading: Simulation and hardware validation: Stairs, steps, and handcarts
sections.summary: Evaluation was conducted in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1. The authors analyzed comparisons with other adaptation methods, applicability across four foundation models, flat-ground behavior, and physical stair/step traversal using onboard depth.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Training and testing were carried out across 4,096 parallel environments in Isaac Lab on challenging terrain tracks featuring stairs (up/down), gaps, platforms, and flat ground.

### Comparison of Adaptation Approaches
The proposed action residual was compared against token residuals (modifying latent commands), LoRA fine-tuning of decoder weights, RL from scratch, and direct depth RL.
- **Adaptation Speed and Stability**: The action residual achieved a 0.947 success rate in just 2k iterations and 0.969 at 20k iterations. In contrast, RL from scratch only succeeded in 1/40 trials on hard terrain, highlighting the benefit of a frozen BFM.
- **Comparison with LoRA**: While LoRA fine-tuning achieved comparable traversal on hard terrain, its flat-ground residual displacement was large at $0.6929$, degrading nominal walking. In contrast, GRAFT's action residual stayed at $0.0520$ on flat ground.
- **Failure of Token Residuals**: Modifying the latent space failed because latent commands still passed through a flat-ground decoder, making it impossible to adjust foot placement and resulting in 0/40 success on obstacles.
- **Impact of Distillation**: While single-stage direct depth RL achieved only a 22/40 success rate, the distilled depth student achieved an impressive 38/40.

### Generalization Across Different Foundation Models
GRAFT was applied to four independent BFMs: SONIC, Humanoid-GPT, HoloMotion, and ScaleBFM. Standalone base models succeeded on hard terrain in only 3/40, 3/40, 8/40, and 2/40 trials, respectively. Adding GRAFT dramatically improved these to 39/40, 34/40, 39/40, and 20/40. This confirms that the residual structure and reward design generalize effectively across diverse BFM architectures.

### Adaptation Cost and Runtime Gating
In simulation across composite terrain (Figure F5), the mean residual rose to 1.529 on obstacle sections but dropped to 0.184 on flat ground. Additionally, disabling the adapter mid-run transitioned smoothly back to standalone BFM tracking without falling, and re-enabling it restored adaptation without instability. Upper-body arm tracking error remained essentially unchanged whether the adapter was active or not.

### Real-World Deployment
Experiments were conducted on a physical Unitree G1 equipped with an onboard depth camera, using unmodified reference walking motions (Figure F6). While the standalone base model stalled and stepped in place before obstacles, the GRAFT-adapted robot raised its feet high to traverse a 0.30 m platform as well as 0.10 m and 0.17 m stairs. It also succeeded in a zero-shot qualitative test crossing an out-of-distribution luggage cart.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: From foot placement to dynamic whole-body balance
sections.summary: GRAFT successfully combines the versatility of frozen foundation models with lightweight residual terrain adaptation. Future work points toward dynamic balance coordination alongside real-time teleoperation and VLA commands beyond recorded motions.
sections.details:
This paper presented GRAFT, a framework that cleanly separates reusable whole-body behavior foundation models (BFMs) from lightweight terrain execution adapters. By letting the frozen BFM handle nominal locomotion and whole-body coordination while the adapter focuses solely on foot clearance and contact placement, complex terrain adaptation is reduced to an efficient learning problem.

Its practicality is supported by substantial traversal improvements across four distinct BFMs, preservation of nominal flat-ground motions, safe runtime gating, and physical humanoid (Unitree G1) experiments using onboard depth.

Current limitations include focusing evaluations primarily on pre-recorded reference motions and restricting corrections to lower-body joints. The authors highlight investigating how lower-body foot placement and balance can coordinate with large upper-body posture changes under live teleoperation and dynamic VLA commands as an exciting future direction.

takeaways: Separating whole-body locomotion generation from terrain-conditioned execution corrections enables rough terrain traversal without modifying foundation model weights.
Adding residuals directly to execution-level joint targets learns faster and preserves flat-ground motions better than modifying latent tokens or fine-tuning weights with LoRA.
Distilling a privileged elevation teacher into an onboard depth student enables smooth zero-shot transfer to real humanoid hardware.
limitations: Because corrections are restricted to lower-body joints, the framework may struggle on extreme terrain requiring drastic upper-body posture adjustments or arm-based balance recovery.
Evaluations currently rely primarily on pre-recorded reference motions; dynamic tracking under real-time teleoperation or evolving VLA commands remains future work.
Performance remains dependent on the underlying BFM's baseline robustness; certain models (like ScaleBFM) plateau earlier on specific terrains such as downward stairs.
